modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Amino Acids of Biological Importance
bookTitle: I- AMINO ACIDS OF BIOLOGICAL IMPORTANCE

concepts.label: An amino acid is placed by holding two classifications at once — its chemical group and whether the body can make it — and no acidic amino acid is essential
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Classify a named amino acid simultaneously by its chemical group and by whether it is essential in the diet.
concepts.definition: Chemically, glycine is the smallest neutral aliphatic amino acid, lysine is basic aliphatic, cystine is the disulfide-linked dimer of the sulfur-containing cysteine, isoleucine is branched-chain, and glutamate is acidic aliphatic. Nutritionally, the nine essential amino acids are valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine, lysine, phenylalanine, tryptophan and histidine; arginine is half-essential; all the rest, including glycine, cysteine and cystine, and glutamate, are non-essential.
concepts.pitfall: Calling cystine essential because methionine, the other sulfur-containing amino acid, is. Methionine is the essential one; cysteine and its dimer cystine are made in the body. There is no essential acidic amino acid at all.
concepts.asked: IV) Match: 1): {1 Mark each} 1 Glycine 2 Lycine 3 Cystine 4 Isoleucine 5 Glutamate — Essential sulfur containing amino acid / Essential branched-chain amino acid / Non-essential smallest amino acid / Non-essential acidic amino acid / Essential basic amino acid / Non-essential sulfur containing amino acid / Essential acidic amino acid

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Carbohydrates of Biological Importance

concepts.label: Cellulose is undigestible because its glucose units are joined by β1,4 bonds, so it acts as dietary bulk that prevents constipation and delays fat absorption
concepts.subject: gi
concepts.objective: Explain why cellulose escapes digestion and state the two dietary consequences the department book gives for it.
concepts.definition: Cellulose is an unbranched chain of β-glucose units joined by β1,4-glucosidic linkages. Amylase hydrolyses only α-linkages, so cellulose passes through the gut undigested. It increases the bulk of food, which stimulates intestinal contractions and prevents constipation, and it delays fat absorption.
concepts.pitfall: Believing that humans secrete a cellulase and simply absorb cellulose slowly. Nothing in the human gut hydrolyses a β1,4 bond — the benefit comes from the cellulose that is never absorbed at all.
concepts.asked: I) Enumerate two of the following: 1) Importance of cellulose {2 Marks}.

concepts.label: GAGs absorb shock because their negatively charged carboxylate and sulfate groups trap water into a gel that is squeezed out under load and reabsorbed when the load is released
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Explain, from the charge on a proteoglycan, how glycosaminoglycans act as shock absorbers in a joint.
concepts.definition: Glycosaminoglycans are long unbranched heteropolysaccharides of repeating amino sugar and uronic acid units, mostly bound to a protein core as proteoglycans. Their negatively charged carboxylate and sulfate groups trap water and create a hydrated gel. When the gel is compressed, water is squeezed out and the molecules occupy a smaller volume; when the compression is released, they regain their original hydrated size. That reversible compressibility is what absorbs shock in joints and makes the eyeball resilient.
concepts.pitfall: Attributing the cushioning to the protein core, or to the sugar chains being physically springy. It is the fixed negative charge holding water that does the work — take the water away and the gel does nothing.
concepts.asked: II) Explain in biochemical basis: 1) GAGs have shock absorbing property {3 Marks}.

concepts.label: Mannitol is the sugar alcohol of mannose, and because the body neither absorbs it well nor metabolises it, it stays osmotically active in the fluid it is given into and is excreted unchanged by the kidney
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Explain, from the fact that mannitol is neither metabolised nor reabsorbed, why it lowers intraocular and intracranial pressure and acts as a diuretic.
concepts.definition: Sugar alcohols are sugars in which the carbonyl group has been reduced to an alcohol group; mannitol is the alcohol of mannose. It is poorly absorbed by the intestines, which is why it serves as a low-calorie sweetener. It is not metabolised in the body and is easily excreted by the kidney, so it remains osmotically active in the compartment it occupies. On that basis it is used as a diuretic, to reduce eye pressure in glaucoma and to reduce intracranial pressure in brain oedema, in each case by osmosis.
concepts.pitfall: Treating it as a drug with a receptor or a transporter to act on. Mannitol has no pharmacological target at all — the whole effect is the osmotic pull of a solute the body cannot dispose of.
concepts.asked: 9) Explain in biochemical basis: Mannitol has a clinical application {4 Marks}.

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Cell Cycle, Apoptosis, and Tumor Suppressor Genes
leaf: Cell Cycle, Apoptosis, and Tumor Suppressor Genes
bookTitle: XIV- CELL CYCLE, APOPTOSIS & TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENES

concepts.label: The proteins of the cell cycle and apoptosis divide into cycle regulators, the p53 guardian, the pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family, and the death receptors that start the extrinsic pathway
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Assign each named protein of the cell cycle and apoptosis to the function it performs.
concepts.definition: Cyclin-dependent kinases are the regulatory proteins that, complexed with cyclins, drive the cell from one phase of the cycle to the next. p53 is the guardian of the genome: it arrests the cycle in G1 through p21 after moderate DNA damage and triggers apoptosis through Bax after severe damage. Bax, Bak and Bok are the apoptotic members of the Bcl-2 family and control cytochrome c release; Bcl-2 and Bcl-x are the anti-apoptotic members. The TNF and FAS receptors initiate the extrinsic pathway when their ligands bind.
concepts.pitfall: Reading Bcl-2 as pro-apoptotic because the whole family is named after it. Bcl-2 itself is the anti-apoptotic member; Bax is the apoptotic one, and under physiological conditions the two are in balance.
concepts.asked: IV) Match: 2): {1 Mark each} 1 CDK 2 P53 3 Bax 4 TNF/FAS receptors 5 Bcl-2 — Anti-Aptotic / Apoptotic / Initiate extrinsic pathway of Apoptosis / Guardian of the Genome / Initiate intrinsic pathway of Apoptosis / Check cell size and cell damage / Regulatory protein in cell cycle

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Chemistry of Free Nucleotides

concepts.label: NAD+, NADP+, FMN and FAD are the nucleotide-derived coenzymes that carry hydrogen between oxidised and reduced forms
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Name the nucleotide coenzymes that carry hydrogen and give the reduced form of each.
concepts.definition: Four nucleotide-derived coenzymes act as hydrogen carriers. NAD+ and NADP+ are nicotinamide dinucleotides reduced to NADH,H+ and NADPH,H+; FMN and FAD are flavin nucleotides reduced to FMNH2 and FADH2. FMN is the only one of the four that contains no adenine.
concepts.pitfall: Adding coenzyme A to the list. Coenzyme A is a nucleotide coenzyme too, but it carries acyl groups on its thiol, not hydrogen.
concepts.asked: I) Enumerate two of the following: 4) Nucleosides that act as a hydrogen carriers {2 Marks}.

concepts.label: Free nucleotides do six different jobs — carry energy, signal as second messengers, donate methyl and sulfate groups, carry hydrogen and carry acyl groups — and which one a nucleotide does is fixed by the group hung on it, not by its base
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Match each free nucleotide or nucleotide derivative to the biochemical role the department book assigns it.
concepts.definition: Beyond being the building blocks of DNA and RNA, free nucleosides and nucleotides serve four families of function. Energy transduction: ATP is the source of energy for mechanical and chemical processes, its bonds between the alpha, beta and gamma phosphates being high-energy bonds, and GTP serves the same role in some pathways. Signalling second messengers: cAMP is formed from ATP by adenylyl cyclase, and cGMP from GTP by guanylyl cyclase, cGMP mediating the smooth-muscle relaxation produced by nitric oxide and other vasodilators. Activated precursors in biosynthesis: S-adenosyl methionine is the most important methyl donor in transmethylation reactions; 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate is used for the synthesis of sulfur-containing compounds such as sulfated glycosaminoglycans and sulfolipids; CDP-choline and UDP-sugars serve phospholipid and glycogen synthesis. Coenzyme components: NAD+, NADP+, FMN and FAD are hydrogen carriers, and coenzyme A is an acyl group carrier through its active thiol group.
concepts.pitfall: Sorting them by their base — reading everything adenine-containing as an energy carrier. PAPS, SAM, FAD, NAD+ and coenzyme A all carry adenine and none of them is an energy source; the group attached to the nucleotide is what determines the function.
concepts.asked: 18) Match: 1 3’-Phosphodenosine-5’-phosphosulfate (PAPS) 2 ATP 3 S-Adenosyl Methionine (SAM) 4 FAD 5 cGMP 6 Coenzyme A — Hydrogen carrier / Methyl donor / Second hormone messenger / Synthesis of sulfur-containing compounds / Acyl group carrier / Source of energy

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Chemistry of Hemoproteins

concepts.label: HbA1c reports three months of glycaemic control because glucose binds haemoglobin non-enzymatically and irreversibly for the whole 120-day life of the red cell
concepts.subject: endo
concepts.objective: Explain why glycated haemoglobin reflects three months of glycaemic control rather than the current blood glucose.
concepts.definition: Part of HbA1 binds blood glucose covalently at the N-terminal valine of the β chain, forming glycated haemoglobin, HbA1c. The reaction is non-enzymatic, so the amount formed depends only on how much glucose the red cell has been exposed to over its 120-day life span. HbA1c is 4 to 6.5% of HbA normally and higher in diabetes mellitus, which is why it reports average control over roughly the preceding three months rather than the glucose at the moment of sampling.
concepts.pitfall: Assuming an enzyme catalyses the glycation and can therefore be saturated or regulated. It is non-enzymatic, which is precisely why the result is a faithful integral of glucose exposure over the red cell's life.
concepts.asked: II) Explain in biochemical basis: 3) HbA1c is used as a test to determine the diabetic control of the patients during the last 3 months {3 Marks}.

concepts.label: The globin chain is what makes haem usable: it dissolves it, keeps its iron from being oxidised, keeps it inside the red cell, and tilts carbon monoxide away from the orientation it would otherwise prefer
concepts.subject: haem
concepts.objective: Give the four functions the globin chain performs for the haem group it carries, and the structural feature responsible for each.
concepts.definition: The globin part of haemoglobin has four functions. It makes haem soluble, because the polar amino acids of the folded chain lie on the surface. It prevents oxidation of haem into haematin, because the haem pocket is lined by nonpolar amino acids, and it also prevents formation of the haem-oxygen-haem complex. It prevents haem diffusing into the plasma, because of its large size. And it reduces the affinity of haem for carbon monoxide: isolated haem binds carbon monoxide with the iron, carbon and oxygen atoms perpendicular to the plane of the ring, but in haemoglobin the distal histidine sterically hinders that orientation, and binding at the less favoured angle weakens the haem-carbon monoxide bond.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the globin merely carries the haem while the haem does all the work. Free haem is insoluble, oxidises to haematin, leaks out of the cell and binds carbon monoxide far more avidly — every one of those problems is solved by the protein around it.
concepts.asked: 11) Explain in biochemical basis: Function of globin (protein) part of hemoglobin {4 Marks}.

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Chemistry of Nucleic Acids

concepts.label: The two strands of the DNA double helix run antiparallel and are held to each other only by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — two for A-T and three for G-C
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: State the orientation of the two DNA strands relative to each other and name the bond that holds them together, with the number of bonds in each base pair.
concepts.definition: Watson and Crick's double helix is the common physiological form of DNA. The two strands run antiparallel, are paired to each other and coil around a common axis to form a right-handed helix. They are held together by complementary base pairing through specific hydrogen bonds: adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds and guanine with cytosine through three. The base pairs inside the helix are stacked above each other by Van der Waals forces and hydrophobic interactions, which stabilise the helix, and the whole resembles a spiral staircase in which the base pairs are the steps and the sugar-phosphate backbones the handrails.
concepts.pitfall: Calling the bond between the two strands covalent because DNA is chemically stable. The phosphodiester bonds along each backbone are covalent; the two strands are held to each other only by hydrogen bonds, which is why heat alone separates them.
concepts.asked: 16) Complete from the following words: {1 Mark each}. [ Parallel - Hydrogen - Antiparallel - Fatherly - Covalent - Maternally - Circular - Linear ] - The 2 DNA strands run a)…………. and are joined by b)……..…… bonds. - Mitochondrial DNA is c)…….…… in shape and d)………….. inherited.

concepts.label: Mitochondrial DNA is a small double-stranded circular supercoil that codes for the machinery of oxidative phosphorylation and is inherited only from the mother, because the mitochondria come from the ovum
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Give the shape, the coding content and the pattern of inheritance of mitochondrial DNA, and say what makes the inheritance maternal.
concepts.definition: DNA is mainly linear, but it is circular in mitochondria, in chloroplasts and in bacteria. Mitochondrial DNA is 0.3 to 1% of the total cellular DNA and human mitochondrial DNA is a small double-stranded circular supercoil. It controls the synthesis of 2 ribosomal RNAs, 22 transfer RNAs and 13 proteins, most of which are involved in oxidative phosphorylation — the electron transport chain and ATP synthesis. Because the mitochondria are provided by the ovum, mitochondrial DNA molecules are maternally inherited and are used to trace maternal lineage. Mutations of mitochondrial DNA are associated with certain types of myopathy.
concepts.pitfall: Explaining maternal inheritance as an X-linked pattern. It has nothing to do with the sex chromosomes — the zygote receives its mitochondria from the ovum, so an affected father transmits nothing and an affected mother transmits to all her children.
concepts.asked: 16) Complete from the following words: {1 Mark each}. […] - Mitochondrial DNA is c)…….…… in shape and d)………….. inherited.

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > DNA Synthesis (Replication) and Repair

concepts.label: The five eukaryotic DNA polymerases divide the work of replication: α primes, β repairs, γ copies mitochondrial DNA, δ makes the lagging strand and ε makes the leading strand
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Name the five eukaryotic DNA polymerases and give the specific job each one does.
concepts.definition: DNA polymerase α, as the α–primase complex, lays down the RNA primers and the short DNA attached to them. DNA polymerase β fills the gap in DNA repair. DNA polymerase γ synthesises mitochondrial DNA. DNA polymerase δ synthesises the lagging strand from many primers, discontinuously as Okazaki fragments. DNA polymerase ε synthesises the leading strand continuously from a single primer. Polymerases δ and ε also proofread by exonuclease activity.
concepts.pitfall: Swapping δ and ε. Epsilon makes the leading strand and needs only one primer; delta makes the lagging strand and needs many.
concepts.asked: I) Enumerate two of the following: 5) DNA polymerases and each one’s importance {2 Marks}.

concepts.label: A replication fork is made by two proteins working together — helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds to open the duplex, and single-strand binding proteins hold the separated strands apart and protect them
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Name the two proteins that open and hold open the parental duplex at a replication fork and state what each contributes.
concepts.definition: Helicase enzyme molecules attach at each origin of replication and unwind the DNA by breaking the hydrogen bonds between the nitrogenous base pairs, producing replication bubbles. Single strand binding (SSB) proteins then bind to the single strands of the unwound DNA and stabilise them; without SSB proteins the two strands would simply rewind, and the proteins also protect the single strand from nucleases that cleave single-stranded DNA. It is the action of helicase and SSB proteins together that creates the replication fork. Topoisomerases relieve the supercoils that unwinding generates ahead of the fork.
concepts.pitfall: Expecting the strands to stay apart once helicase has passed. Complementary single strands re-anneal spontaneously; the SSB proteins are what keep the template available, which is why they are drawn coating the separated strands rather than sitting at the fork apex.
concepts.asked: 20) Diagram (2) [Elongation of DNA]. a) Name of (1) and mention its function. b) Name of (2) and mention its function. c) Name of (3): ……………….

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Enzymes

concepts.label: The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction is set by substrate concentration, enzyme concentration, cofactor concentration, temperature and pH
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Name the five factors that affect the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction and say what limits the reaction once each is in excess.
concepts.definition: Five factors govern the velocity of an enzyme-catalysed reaction: substrate concentration, which raises velocity to Vmax as the enzyme saturates; enzyme concentration, to which velocity is directly proportional until substrate becomes limiting; cofactor concentration, on the same terms; temperature, rising to an optimum near 37 °C and stopping near 70 °C as the enzyme denatures; and pH, most enzymes having an optimum between 5 and 9.
concepts.pitfall: Treating higher temperature as simply faster. Above the optimum the enzyme protein denatures and the catalytic site is disorganised, so velocity falls rather than rises.
concepts.asked: I) Enumerate two of the following: 3) Factors affecting the rate of enzyme catalyzed reaction {2 Marks}.

concepts.label: Sulfonamides are bacteriostatic because they are structural analogues of PABA and competitively inhibit the bacterial enzyme that builds folic acid from it
concepts.subject: pharm
concepts.objective: Explain how the structural similarity of a sulfonamide to PABA produces a bacteriostatic effect, and classify the type of enzyme inhibition involved.
concepts.definition: Bacteria must synthesise their own folic acid, and they build it from para-aminobenzoic acid. Sulfonamides are structurally similar to PABA, so they compete with it for the active site of the enzyme that uses PABA as substrate. Folate synthesis stops, growth and multiplication stop, and the bacteria are held rather than killed — a bacteriostatic action.
concepts.pitfall: Calling it bactericidal, or expecting it to work on human cells too. Humans take folate in the diet rather than synthesising it from PABA, so the target enzyme is not there to inhibit — that selectivity is the whole point.
concepts.asked: II) Explain in biochemical basis: 4) Sulfonamides are bacteriostatic agents {3 Marks}.

concepts.label: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate closely enough to occupy the active site, so it raises the apparent Km without touching Vmax and is defeated by adding more substrate
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Explain how structural similarity to the substrate produces reversible inhibition, state what it does to Km and Vmax, and give two worked examples.
concepts.definition: A competitive inhibitor is structurally similar to the substrate, so it competes with the substrate to bind reversibly at the active or catalytic site. The degree of inhibition depends on the ratio of inhibitor concentration to substrate concentration rather than on the absolute concentration of either, and on their relative affinities for the enzyme. Vmax is unaffected, because the inhibition is reversed by raising substrate concentration and at a high enough substrate concentration the reaction reaches the same Vmax as in the absence of inhibitor. The apparent Km rises, because more substrate is needed to reach half of Vmax. The department book's examples are allopurinol, a structural analogue of hypoxanthine that inhibits xanthine oxidase and is used in gout; sulfonamides, structural analogues of para-aminobenzoic acid that block bacterial folate synthesis; and dicumarol and warfarin, structurally similar to a vitamin K derivative and used as anticoagulants.
concepts.pitfall: Confusing it with allosteric inhibition because both are reversible. An allosteric inhibitor binds away from the catalytic site, changes the protein's conformation, and cannot be outcompeted by more substrate; a competitive inhibitor can.
concepts.asked: 12) Explain in biochemical basis: Competitive inhibitors has an inhibitory functions on enzymes, explain how and enumerate 2 examples {4 Marks}.

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Lipids of Biological Importance

concepts.label: Snake venom is toxic because its lecithinase has phospholipase A2 activity, converting red cell membrane phospholipids to lysophospholipids and rupturing the membrane
concepts.subject: mul
concepts.objective: Explain the enzymatic mechanism by which snake venom haemolyses red cells and name the class of enzyme responsible.
concepts.definition: Snake venom toxins contain a lecithinase with phospholipase A2 activity. Injected into the blood, it hydrolyses the phospholipids of red cell membranes into lysophospholipids. Lysophospholipids do not hold a bilayer together, so the membrane ruptures and the cell haemolyses. Untreated, snake venom toxins cause death; the treatment is antitoxin.
concepts.pitfall: Naming phospholipase D. Phospholipase D is absent from humans and is a plant enzyme; the venom's activity is phospholipase A2, which is why the product is a lysophospholipid.
concepts.asked: II) Explain in biochemical basis: 2) Snake venom is toxic {3 Marks}.

concepts.label: Eicosanoid synthesis runs from membrane phospholipid through phospholipase A2 to arachidonic acid, which prostaglandin H synthase turns into the cyclic products and lipoxygenase into the acyclic ones
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Name the three enzymes of the eicosanoid pathway and say which class of eicosanoid each one produces.
concepts.definition: Eicosanoids are C20 polyunsaturated fatty acid derivatives. Phospholipase A2 liberates arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids. Prostaglandin H synthase, which carries both cyclooxygenase and peroxidase activity, converts arachidonic acid into the cyclic compounds — prostaglandins, prostacyclins and thromboxanes. Lipoxygenase converts it into the acyclic compounds, the leukotrienes and lipoxins.
concepts.pitfall: Treating cyclooxygenase and prostaglandin H synthase as two different enzymes at two points of the pathway. Cyclooxygenase is one of the two catalytic activities of prostaglandin H synthase; peroxidase is the other.
concepts.asked: III) Diagrams: -Diagram (1) [Pathway of Eicosanoids synthesis]. {6 Marks} 1) ....……………….. {1 Mark} 2) ....……………….. {1 Mark} 3) ....……………….. {1 Mark} a) Explain how (SAIDs) can be anti-inflammatory. {1 Mark} b) Explain how (NSAIDs) can be anti-inflammatory. {1 Mark} c) Explain how (Singular) can treat bronchial asthmatic attacks. {1 Mark}

concepts.label: The three anti-inflammatory drug classes act at three different points of the eicosanoid pathway — steroids on phospholipase A2, NSAIDs on cyclooxygenase, and Singulair on the leukotriene receptor
concepts.subject: pharm
concepts.objective: Locate each anti-inflammatory drug class on the eicosanoid pathway and explain why blocking that point produces its particular effect.
concepts.definition: Steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as hydrocortisone, prednisone and betamethasone inhibit phospholipase A2 and so reduce the supply of arachidonic acid to the whole pathway. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as aspirin, indomethacin and ibuprofen inhibit cyclooxygenase activity and so block prostaglandin synthesis alone. Singulair is a leukotriene receptor antagonist: it does not inhibit an enzyme but blocks the receptor, relieving the bronchospasm that leukotrienes cause and inhibiting the allergic pathway.
concepts.pitfall: Assuming an NSAID is simply a weaker steroid acting at the same place. A steroid shuts off arachidonic acid for both branches; an NSAID leaves the lipoxygenase branch running, which is why it does not relieve leukotriene-driven bronchospasm.
concepts.asked: III) Diagram (1) a) Explain how (SAIDs) can be anti-inflammatory. {1 Mark} b) Explain how (NSAIDs) can be anti-inflammatory. {1 Mark} c) Explain how (Singular) can treat bronchial asthmatic attacks. {1 Mark}

concepts.label: Cholesterol matters because almost nothing else can be made without it — the bile acids, every steroid hormone and vitamin D3 all come from it, and it is the constituent that controls the fluidity of the cell membrane
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Name the derivatives cholesterol gives rise to and state its structural role in the cell membrane.
concepts.definition: Cholesterol is the most important animal sterol; free cholesterol contains 27 carbon atoms and it circulates either free or esterified with a fatty acid. It is converted into bile acids and bile salts in the liver. It is the precursor of all the steroid hormones — the sex hormones and the corticoids. It is oxidised in the liver into 7-dehydrocholesterol, which ultraviolet light converts into vitamin D3 in the skin. And it is an important constituent of cell membranes, controlling their fluidity. It is excreted mainly in the bile as bile salts.
concepts.pitfall: Filing cholesterol only as the substance that causes atherosclerosis. Every steroid hormone, both bile acid classes and vitamin D3 are built from it, and a cell that could not make it would have no membrane worth the name.
concepts.asked: 10) Explain in biochemical basis: Cholesterol is an important sterol and has many derivatives {4 Marks}.

concepts.label: Membrane fluidity is set by how closely the phospholipid tails can pack: a cis-double bond kinks the chain and keeps them apart, a saturated chain is straight and lets them pack, and cholesterol sits between them controlling the result
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Identify cholesterol and the saturated and unsaturated fatty acid chains on a bilayer diagram and explain, from chain shape and packing, why each raises or lowers fluidity.
concepts.definition: Phospholipids are amphipathic, with non-polar fatty acid side chains and polar head groups, and they are the important constituents of the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane. Increasing the unsaturated fatty acid content at carbon 2 of the phospholipids increases membrane fluidity, because the kinks produced by the cis-double bonds prevent the phospholipids from packing closely together. Saturated fatty acid chains carry no such kink, so they lie straight and pack closely, and closer packing means lower fluidity. Cholesterol is an important constituent of cell membranes that controls their fluidity, and it sits among the phospholipids of the bilayer.
concepts.pitfall: Treating the double bond itself as what loosens the membrane. It is the geometry it imposes — a cis-double bond bends the chain, and a bent chain cannot lie flat against its neighbours; a trans-double bond leaves the chain straight and does not have the same effect.
concepts.asked: 19) Diagram (1) [Phospholipid bilayer]. 1) ....………….. 2) ....………….. 3) ....………….. a) Explain why (2) increases the membrane fluidity. b) Explain why (3) decreases the membrane fluidity.

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Protein Synthesis (Translation)

concepts.label: Covalent post-translational modification adds a functional group to an amino acid residue — phosphate, carbohydrate, acetyl or methyl, hydroxyl or carboxyl — and each has its own worked example
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Name the types of covalent post-translational modification and give the department book's example for each.
concepts.definition: Amino acid residues in a finished chain are modified enzymatically to alter activity or stability, to direct the protein to a compartment, or to prepare it for secretion. Phosphorylation and dephosphorylation on serine, threonine or tyrosine regulate the enzymes of glycogen metabolism and regulators of gene transcription. Glycosylation marks proteins destined for secretion, lysosomes or membranes. Acetylation or methylation of the N-terminal residue alters charge, as in chromatin remodelling by histone acetylation. Hydroxylation of prolyl and lysyl residues stabilises collagen. Carboxylation forms γ-carboxyglutamate, which lets clotting proteins bind calcium.
concepts.pitfall: Offering trimming — the conversion of pre-proinsulin to insulin — as a covalent modification. Trimming is proteolytic removal of a segment and is the other branch of post-translational modification, not this one.
concepts.asked: I) Enumerate two of the following: 6) Post-translational covalent modification, and an example each {2 Marks}.

concepts.label: A base substitution in a coding region is nonsense if it creates a stop codon, missense if it changes the amino acid, and silent if the new codon is a synonym
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Name the three types of point mutation in a coding region and explain how each affects the protein product.
concepts.definition: Base substitutions are the commonest gene mutations. A nonsense mutation converts an amino acid codon into a stop codon, so translation terminates prematurely and the protein product is usually non-functional — thalassaemia is the example. A missense mutation changes the codon so a different amino acid is inserted; the effect ranges from none to very serious, as in sickle cell anaemia, where glutamate is replaced by valine at position six of the β chain. A silent mutation gives a synonym codon for the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged.
concepts.pitfall: Assuming every missense mutation is harmless because only one amino acid changes. Whether it matters depends on which amino acid — swapping polar glutamate for nonpolar valine creates the sticky patch that produces sickle cell anaemia.
concepts.asked: III) Diagrams: -Diagram (3) [Point mutation types]. {5 Marks} 1) ………………… {0.5 Mark} a) Explain how this type could produce severe damage. {1.5 Marks} 2) ………………… {0.5 Mark} a) Explain how this type could produce severe damage. {1.5 Marks} 3) ………………… {0.5 Mark} a) Mention its effect. {0.5 Mark}

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Proteins of Biological Importance

concepts.label: Denaturation ruptures the bonds holding secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, leaving the primary sequence intact but the protein insoluble, more viscous, more digestible and biologically dead
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: List the effects of denaturation on a protein and say which level of structure survives it.
concepts.definition: Denaturation breaks the bonds that stabilise the secondary, tertiary and quaternary orders, leaving only the primary structure. The protein loses solubility as its nonpolar groups become exposed, viscosity rises, digestibility by proteolytic enzymes rises because peptide bonds are exposed, biological activity is lost, and antigenic property is lost.
concepts.pitfall: Saying the peptide bonds are broken. Denaturation leaves the primary structure untouched — that is why a denatured protein is more digestible rather than already digested.
concepts.asked: I) Enumerate two of the following: 2) Effects of denaturation of protein {2 Marks}.

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Proteins of Extracellular Matrix

concepts.label: Collagen is strong because every level of its structure is built for tightness — three residues per turn, glycine in every third position, a right-handed superhelix of left-handed chains, hydroxyproline hydrogen bonds, and covalent cross-links between chains
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Give the structural features, from the repeating triplet up to the fibre, that account for the tensile strength of collagen.
concepts.definition: The building unit of collagen is tropocollagen: three left-handed alpha-chains twisted into a right-handed superhelix, each chain about a thousand amino acids of the repeating triplet Gly-X-Y, where X is proline and Y hydroxyproline. Seven features give it its strength. Each turn contains only three amino acid residues, making a tight helix where an ordinary protein has 3.6. Glycine, in every third position, has a side chain short enough to let the chains lie very close together. The three left-handed chains form a right-handed superhelix. The high hydroxyproline content forms hydrogen bonds between chains. Covalent cross-links between adjacent chains give the tensile property, so collagen can be stretched without breaking. The molecules are arranged specifically into fibrils and then fibres. And the staggered, overhanging array gives collagen marked flexibility.
concepts.pitfall: Attributing the strength to proline alone. Proline prevents a right-handed helix from forming in the individual chain, but it is glycine at every third position that lets three chains pack close enough to wind together, and the covalent cross-links that let the result be pulled without breaking.
concepts.asked: 13) Explain in biochemical basis: Collagen has a strong structure {4 Marks}.

modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > RNA Synthesis (Transcription)

concepts.label: Splicing removes introns and joins exons using the snRNP spliceosome, and splicing the same primary transcript differently yields several proteins from one gene
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Identify the post-transcriptional steps on the pathway diagram, name the ribonucleoproteins that carry out splicing, and explain what alternative splicing achieves.
concepts.definition: The primary transcript, hnRNA, contains introns that do not code for amino acids lying between the coding exons. Splicing removes the introns and joins the exons to give functional mRNA, and it requires a spliceosome made of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins — snRNPs, built of special proteins and small nuclear RNAs. Alternative splicing splices the same primary transcript in different ways to yield different proteins from one gene, which is why the number of proteins far exceeds the number of genes.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking alternative splicing is a fault that produces a wrong protein. It is a normal, regulated route by which one gene legitimately encodes several different products — the antibody genes are the department book's example.
concepts.asked: III) Diagrams: -Diagram (2) [Post-transcriptional modifications]. {5 Marks} 1) ....……………….. {1 Mark} 2) ....……………….. {1 Mark} a) Mention the ribonucleoproteins responsible. {0.5 Mark} b) Mention a disease related. {0.5 Mark} 3) ....……………….. {1 Mark} a) Mention its importance. {1 Mark}

concepts.label: The two promoter boxes divide the work — TATA says where transcription starts and CAAT and GC say how often — while TFIIH opens the strands, polyadenylation sets how long the message lives, and alternative splicing decides how many proteins the gene yields
concepts.subject: fnd
concepts.objective: Assign each promoter element, transcription factor and processing step to the specific job it does in the making of a mature messenger RNA.
concepts.definition: RNA polymerase II synthesises messenger RNA, most small nuclear RNAs and micro RNAs. The eukaryotic promoter carries two basal expression elements: the TATA box, of sequence TATAAA and 20 to 30 base pairs upstream of the start site, which defines where transcription is to start along the DNA; and the CAAT box and GC box, 40 to 200 base pairs upstream, which define when transcription starts and so control how frequently the event occurs. TFIID binds the TATA box first and the other transcription factors and RNA polymerase II assemble on it to form the pre-initiation complex; TFIIH then separates the two DNA strands by its helicase activity and activates RNA polymerase II. After transcription, the primary transcript is capped at the 5' end, polyadenylated at the 3' end by poly(A) polymerase — and the length of the poly(A) tail determines the half-life of the mRNA — spliced, and edited. Alternative splicing splices the primary transcript of some genes differently to yield different proteins from one gene, which explains why the estimated number of proteins much exceeds the number of genes.
concepts.pitfall: Reading the TATA box and the CAAT box as two names for the same thing because both are upstream promoter elements. TATA fixes the start point and CAAT and GC set the frequency; a mutation in one changes where transcription begins and in the other changes how much message is made.
concepts.asked: 17) Match: 1 mRNA 2 CAAT box and GC box 3 Polyadenylation of mRNA at 3’ end 4 TATA box 5 TFIIH 6 Alternative splicing — Explains why the estimated number of proteins much exceeds the number of genes / Has helicase and kinase activity / Control how frequently this event occurs / Determines the half-life time of mRNA / Synthesized by RNA polymerase II / Defines where transcription is to start along the DNA

modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Autonomic ganglia

concepts.label: There are four types of autonomic ganglion — the paravertebral sympathetic chain, the collateral ganglia, the terminal ganglia, and the adrenal medulla as a modified sympathetic ganglion
concepts.subject: neuro
concepts.objective: Name the four types of autonomic ganglion, give the site of each, and say which division of the autonomic nervous system relays there.
concepts.definition: The paravertebral sympathetic chain lies on both sides of the vertebral column with a ganglion for each spinal segment, except the cervical region, which has only three — superior, middle and inferior; it relays sympathetic fibres only. The collateral ganglia lie midway between cord and viscera at the origins of the large branches of the abdominal aorta and are named after them: coeliac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric relay sympathetic fibres, while the ciliary, sphenopalatine, submaxillary and otic ganglia relay parasympathetic fibres. The terminal ganglia lie near or within the organ itself and relay parasympathetic fibres, whose postganglionic axons are only a millimetre to a few centimetres long. The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion whose postganglionic cells have lost their axons and secrete catecholamines into the blood.
concepts.pitfall: Assuming every collateral ganglion is sympathetic because the abdominal ones are. The ciliary, sphenopalatine, submaxillary and otic ganglia are collateral ganglia that relay parasympathetic fibres.
concepts.asked: 3) Mention types of autonomic ganglia {8 Marks}.

modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Chemical transmission at autonomic junctions and autonomic receptors
leaf: Chemical transmission at autonomic junctions and autonomic receptors
bookTitle: Chemical transmission at autonomic junctions & autonomic receptors

concepts.label: Adrenergic receptors sit both on the effector organ and on the nerve ending that released the transmitter, and the two alpha and three beta subtypes are told apart by which second messenger they move and which plain muscle they act on
concepts.subject: neuro
concepts.objective: Give the presynaptic and postsynaptic distribution of adrenergic receptors, the second messenger each subtype uses, and the organ effect of each subtype.
concepts.definition: There are two major types of adrenergic receptor, alpha with subtypes 1 and 2, and beta with subtypes 1, 2 and 3. Presynaptically they are autoreceptors on the membrane of postganglionic adrenergic nerve endings that regulate transmitter release: stimulating presynaptic alpha receptors decreases noradrenaline release and stimulating presynaptic beta receptors increases it. Postsynaptically, alpha-1 acts by raising intracellular calcium, alpha-2 by inhibiting adenylyl cyclase and lowering cAMP, and beta-1 and beta-2 by stimulating adenylyl cyclase and raising cAMP. Alpha-1 receptors are mainly excitatory and contract plain muscle: vasoconstriction in skin, viscera and male genitalia, the dilator pupillae producing mydriasis, the splenic capsule, the gastrointestinal sphincters retaining faeces, the internal urethral sphincter retaining urine, and the seminal vesicles and vas deferens in ejaculation. Alpha-2 receptors are mainly inhibitory and relax intestinal plain muscle. Beta-1 receptors are mainly excitatory and accelerate the heart and increase its force of contraction. Beta-2 receptors are mainly inhibitory and relax plain muscle: vasodilatation of coronary and skeletal-muscle vessels, bronchodilatation, and relaxation of gut, urinary bladder and uterus. Beta-3 receptors drive lipolysis.
concepts.pitfall: Assuming alpha always constricts and beta always dilates everywhere. Alpha-2 relaxes intestinal plain muscle and beta-1 excites the heart; the subtype, not the letter, decides whether the effect is excitatory or inhibitory.
concepts.asked: 3) Explain distribution and action of adrenergic receptors {9 Marks}.

concepts.label: Autonomic fibres are named for the transmitter they release: cholinergic fibres are every preganglionic fibre, every postganglionic parasympathetic fibre and two sympathetic exceptions, and adrenergic fibres are all the remaining postganglionic sympathetic ones, which secrete noradrenaline
concepts.subject: neuro
concepts.objective: Say which autonomic fibres are cholinergic and which are adrenergic, and name the transmitter each releases.
concepts.definition: Acetylcholine and noradrenaline are the main chemical transmitters at autonomic synaptic junctions, so autonomic nerve fibres are divided into cholinergic and adrenergic. Cholinergic fibres are all preganglionic autonomic fibres, sympathetic and parasympathetic alike including those to the adrenal medulla; all postganglionic parasympathetic fibres; and two groups of postganglionic sympathetic fibres, the secretory fibres to sweat glands and the vasodilator fibres to the blood vessels of skeletal muscle. All the other postganglionic sympathetic fibres are adrenergic and secrete noradrenaline, which is also secreted with adrenaline from the adrenal medulla. Cholinergic receptors are activated by acetylcholine and adrenergic receptors by noradrenaline.
concepts.pitfall: Calling every sympathetic postganglionic fibre adrenergic. The sudomotor fibres to sweat glands and the vasodilator fibres to skeletal-muscle vessels are sympathetic and cholinergic, which is why sweating is a sympathetic response blocked by an antimuscarinic.
concepts.asked: 7) Adrenergic nerve fibers secrete: A. Acetyl choline B. Noradrenaline C. Dopamine D. Calcium ions

modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Parasympathetic nervous system

concepts.label: The vagus carries the whole parasympathetic supply of the thoracic and abdominal viscera, slowing the atria, constricting bronchi, driving gut motility and secretion, and emptying the gall bladder
concepts.subject: neuro
concepts.objective: Give the origin, course and relay of the vagal parasympathetic supply and state its effect on the heart, lungs, gastrointestinal tract and gall bladder.
concepts.definition: Preganglionic fibres arise from the vagal nucleus in the medulla oblongata, run in the vagus to supply the entire thoracic and abdominal viscera — about 75% of all parasympathetic fibres — and relay in terminal ganglia in or close to the organ. On the heart the vagus does not supply the ventricles; it inhibits all properties of atrial muscle only, and decreases coronary blood flow and oxygen consumption. On the lungs it produces bronchoconstriction, dilatation of the pulmonary vessels and stimulation of the bronchial glands. On the gastrointestinal tract it contracts the plain muscle of oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and proximal large intestine, relaxes the sphincters, and is secretory to the gut glands, liver and pancreas. On the gall bladder it contracts the wall and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, evacuating it.
concepts.pitfall: Saying the vagus slows the whole heart. It does not supply the ventricles at all — it inhibits the properties of atrial muscle only.
concepts.asked: 4) Explain function of parasympathetic system on Thoracic & Abdominal viscera {6 Marks}.

modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Sympathetic nervous system

concepts.label: The sympathetic system discharges as one unit in an emergency, and everything it does — dilating the pupil, accelerating the heart, constricting skin vessels, raising alertness, freeing glucose and fatty acids — is a preparation for flight, fear or fight
concepts.subject: neuro
concepts.objective: List the components of the sympathetic alarm response and say, for each, what advantage it gives in an emergency.
concepts.definition: The sympathetic nervous system is the catabolic, energy-consuming system, and in emergency it discharges as a single unit to prepare the individual for flight, fear or fight. It dilates the pupils, letting more light into the eyes. It accelerates the heartbeat and raises the blood pressure, giving better perfusion of vital organs and muscles. It constricts the blood vessels of the skin, which limits bleeding from wounds. It lowers the threshold in the reticular formation of the brain, reinforcing the alert and aroused state. It stimulates lipolysis and glycogenolysis, supplying more glucose and free fatty acids. In the lungs the same discharge produces bronchodilatation, so airway resistance falls while almost every other parameter rises.
concepts.pitfall: Expecting every sympathetic effect to be an increase. Bronchodilatation lowers airway resistance and the gut wall relaxes — the discharge is uniform in purpose, not in direction.
concepts.asked: 6) While driving, you narrowly avoid a car accident by slamming on the brakes. Your heart rate is accelerated (increased) when you come to a stop. Which of the following physiologic parameters will be decreased in response to this experience? A. Airway resistance B. Pupil dilatation C. Systolic blood pressure. D. Vascular resistance

modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Blood > Physiological limitations of blood coagulation

concepts.label: Coagulation is held in check by general limiting reactions — smooth endothelium, hepatic clearance of activated factors and natural heparin — and by three specific ones: the thromboxane–prostacyclin balance, antithrombin III, and the fibrinolytic system
concepts.subject: haem
concepts.objective: Explain the general and specific reactions that stop coagulation spreading beyond the site of injury, and name the factors each one inactivates.
concepts.definition: The tendency of blood to clot is balanced in vivo by limiting reactions. The general ones are the smooth vascular endothelium, which activates neither factor XII nor platelets; removal and inactivation of activated clotting factors in the liver; and naturally occurring heparin. The specific ones are the balance between the aggregating, vasoconstrictor thromboxane A2 and the anti-aggregating, vasodilator prostacyclin, which confines the clot to the injury; antithrombin III, which inhibits activated factors IX, X, XI and XII and is facilitated by heparin; and the fibrinolytic system, in which thrombin bound to endothelial thrombomodulin activates protein C, which with protein S inactivates factors V and VIII and releases tissue plasminogen activator, so plasmin lyses fibrin to fibrin degradation products that themselves inhibit thrombin.
concepts.pitfall: Treating this as a list of anticoagulant drugs. These are the body's own limiting reactions; warfarin and administered heparin are the pharmacological answer to a different question.
concepts.asked: 2) Explain physiological limitations of blood coagulation {9 Marks}.

modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Blood > Plasma proteins

concepts.label: The liver makes albumin, fibrinogen, the clotting factors and half the globulins while plasma cells make the gamma globulins, and between them the plasma proteins hold water in the capillary, buffer the blood, defend it, clot it, thicken it, seal the capillary pores, carry small molecules and store amino acids
concepts.subject: haem
concepts.objective: State where each class of plasma protein is formed and give six functions of the plasma proteins, naming which protein is responsible for each.
concepts.definition: Plasma proteins are present at 7.2 to 7.4 g/dl and consist of albumin, globulins, fibrinogen and the other coagulation factors. The liver is the main site of synthesis, making albumin, fibrinogen, the coagulation factors and 50% of the globulins; the gamma globulins are made by plasma cells in lymphoid tissue. They contribute only 25 to 28 mmHg of the 5000 mmHg total plasma osmotic pressure, but the capillary wall is impermeable to them, so that small contribution is the effective colloidal osmotic pressure that draws tissue fluid back into the blood, and albumin dominates it because it is the most concentrated. They supply 15% of the buffering power of blood; the gamma globulins provide humoral immunity; fibrinogen and the clotting factors coagulate the blood; fibrinogen also contributes most to blood viscosity because of its elongated shape; plasma proteins close the pores of the capillary wall and so set capillary permeability; albumin and the alpha and beta globulins carry hormones, vitamins, lipids and minerals and stop them being lost in urine; and they are a reserve of amino acids for tissue protein.
concepts.pitfall: Reading the small share of total osmotic pressure as a small effect. Crystalloids account for almost all of the 5000 mmHg, but they cross the capillary wall freely and so exert no net pull; the 25 to 28 mmHg of the proteins is the only part that acts across the capillary, which is why oedema follows hypoalbuminaemia.
concepts.asked: 1) Regarding plasma proteins, explain site of formation {2 Marks}, mention six functions {6 Marks}.

modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Blood > Platelets and haemostasis

concepts.label: Thromboxane A2 from the platelet and prostacyclin from the endothelium are made by the same enzyme from the same substrate and do the opposite things, and that opposition is what keeps a platelet plug at the site of injury
concepts.subject: haem
concepts.objective: Compare thromboxane A2 and prostacyclin by their cell of origin and their three actions each, and explain what the balance between them achieves.
concepts.definition: Thromboxane A2 is produced from arachidonic acid in the membrane of activated platelets by cyclooxygenase. It is a vasoconstrictor, a stimulator of the platelet release reaction and a powerful stimulant of platelet aggregation. Prostacyclin is produced from arachidonic acid in the endothelium of blood vessels by the same cyclooxygenase. It is a powerful vasodilator and an inhibitor of both platelet release and platelet aggregation. Because its actions are the opposite of those of thromboxane A2, prostacyclin keeps the platelet plug localised to the site of injury, and the balance between the two is one of the physiological limitations of blood coagulation.
concepts.pitfall: Treating the two as products of different pathways because their effects are opposite. Both come from arachidonic acid through the same cyclooxygenase step; only the cell differs, and that is exactly why one drug acting on that step can shift the balance.
concepts.asked: 2) Compare between function of TXA2 and PGI2 {6 Marks}, and function of aspirin in preventing myocardial infarction {3 Marks}.

concepts.label: Aspirin prevents myocardial infarction because it inhibits cyclooxygenase in both cells but only the endothelial cell can make the enzyme again, so a small prolonged dose suppresses thromboxane A2 while prostacyclin recovers
concepts.subject: pharm
concepts.objective: Explain why inhibiting an enzyme common to both platelet and endothelium produces a net antithrombotic effect, and why the dose has to be small and prolonged.
concepts.definition: Aspirin inhibits the cyclooxygenase enzyme and therefore reduces production of both thromboxane A2 and prostacyclin. The endothelial cell produces new cyclooxygenase within a matter of hours, whereas the platelet cannot manufacture the enzyme at all. Administration of small amounts of aspirin for prolonged periods therefore reduces clot formation and has been of value in preventing myocardial infarction.
concepts.pitfall: Assuming a bigger dose gives better protection. A larger dose suppresses endothelial prostacyclin as well, and the protective effect comes from the asymmetry between a cell that can replace the enzyme and one that cannot.
concepts.asked: 2) …and function of aspirin in preventing myocardial infarction {3 Marks}.

modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Blood > Vitamin B12 and folic acid

concepts.label: Vitamin B12 is absorbed only after intrinsic factor from the gastric parietal cells binds it and carries it to a receptor in the lower ileum
concepts.subject: haem
concepts.objective: Describe the steps of vitamin B12 absorption from gastric secretion of intrinsic factor to storage in the liver.
concepts.definition: The parietal cells of the gastric glands secrete intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein that combines with vitamin B12 and protects it from digestion. Intrinsic factor also binds the vitamin to a specific receptor on the brush border of the mucosal cells of the lower ileum. Trypsin from the pancreas is required, so pancreatic disease impairs absorption. The vitamin enters the intestinal cell with intrinsic factor by pinocytosis, is set free inside, crosses the epithelium, and travels in the blood bound to transcobalamin II; the excess is stored in the liver.
concepts.pitfall: Expecting a dietary deficiency. Except in vegetarians, B12 deficiency is a failure of absorption — no intrinsic factor, no ileum, or no trypsin — not a shortage in the diet, and the liver holds several years' store either way.
concepts.asked: 1) Explain absorption of Vitamin B12 {3 Marks}, mentioning its importance {2 Marks} and the manifestations of its deficiency {2 Marks}.

concepts.label: Vitamin B12 is needed for DNA synthesis and for myelination, so its deficiency gives both a macrocytic anaemia and neurological signs
concepts.subject: haem
concepts.objective: State why vitamin B12 is needed for erythropoiesis and predict the two families of manifestation its deficiency produces.
concepts.definition: Vitamin B12 is required to form thymidine triphosphate, a building block of DNA, so it is essential for the nuclear maturation and division of the rapidly dividing bone marrow cells and hence for erythropoiesis. It is also needed for the myelination of nerves. Its deficiency therefore gives a macrocytic anaemia — the red cells grow bigger, irregular in shape and very fragile because nuclear maturation and cell division fail while cytoplasm keeps growing — together with neurological manifestations.
concepts.pitfall: Explaining the large cells as a sign that the marrow is working harder. The cells are large because the nucleus cannot mature and divide while the cytoplasm goes on growing — failure of division, not compensation.
concepts.asked: 1) … mentioning its importance {2 Marks} and the manifestations of its deficiency {2 Marks}.
